meta.title: Cacio e Pepe (The Right Way)
meta.description: Three ingredients, zero margin for error. The deceptively simple Roman pasta that humbles experienced cooks.

children.value: Cacio e pepe has three ingredients: pasta, Pecorino Romano, and black pepper. No cream. No butter. No parmesan. The sauce comes from emulsifying cheese with starchy pasta water. It sounds trivial. It is not.
Read the entire recipe before cooking. Cacio e pepe fails when the timing is off — you need everything ready before the pasta is done. There is no 'hold' step.
Ingredients (serves 2)
200g tonnarelli or spaghetti
150g Pecorino Romano, finely grated
(use a Microplane — the fine powder melts smoothly)
2 tsp freshly cracked black pepper (coarse)
Salt for pasta water
Do not substitute pre-grated cheese. The anti-caking agents (cellulose, potato starch) prevent proper emulsification. Your sauce will be grainy instead of creamy. Grate it yourself on a Microplane.
Method

attrs.title: Boil pasta in less water than usual

children.value: Use a narrower, taller pot with about 2 liters of water for 200g of pasta. This concentrates the starch in the water, which is critical for the sauce. Salt it aggressively — it should taste like the sea.

While the water heats, add the cracked black pepper to a cold, dry pan (large enough to hold the pasta later). Toast over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until fragrant and slightly smoking. Add a ladle of pasta water and let it simmer to infuse — this blooms the pepper's aromatics.
Put the grated Pecorino in a bowl. Gradually add
cold
pasta water (yes, cold — take it before it boils) a tablespoon at a time, stirring constantly until you have a thick, smooth paste like cake frosting. This pre-hydration prevents clumping.
Pull the pasta 2 minutes before al dente. Transfer it directly to the pepper pan with tongs (some water clinging to the pasta is good). Toss vigorously over
low heat
for 1 minute, adding splashes of pasta water to keep it loose.
Kill the heat completely

. Wait 30 seconds for the pan to cool slightly (too hot and the cheese seizes into clumps). Add the cheese paste and toss aggressively, adding tiny splashes of hot pasta water until the sauce is silky and coats each strand. Serve immediately — this sauce waits for no one.
If the cheese clumps, the pan was too hot. Rescue it by adding more pasta water and tossing off-heat. It won't be perfect but it'll be edible. Next time, wait longer after killing the heat.
The Science

Cacio e pepe is an emulsion — fat (from the cheese) suspended in water (starchy pasta water) stabilized by protein (also from the cheese). The starch acts as an additional emulsifier, preventing the fat from separating.
This is why the details matter:
Concentrated pasta water
= more starch = better emulsification
Finely grated cheese
= higher surface area = melts evenly
Temperature control
= Pecorino's proteins denature above ~170°F/76°C, causing clumping
Aggressive tossing
= mechanical emulsification, like shaking a vinaigrette
Three ingredients, five minutes of active cooking, a lifetime to master. That's the beauty of Roman pasta.
